h: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר, מַאֲמָר א׳ Rosh Chodesh Adar — Maamar Aleph

p: "They were days of miracles for Yisrael,
that from when Adar enters we increase,
אֲבָל מִלְּשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא אַחַר כָּךְ [כט, ב]
But from the Gemara's wording afterward (29b),
"let him make himself available in Adar,
it implies that it refers to Adar specifically.
The matter is that the derivation is from Av:
just as in the month of Av,
in which there was one day
on which mourning and weeping occurred,
we diminish in joy from Rosh Chodesh,
as they derived in the Gemara (there, 30a):
the one who holds that the entire month,
all of it, is forbidden derives it from "her new moon" —
in which a day of joy occurred,
the joy is from Rosh Chodesh
וְכֵן נִזְכַּר גַּם בַּפָּסוּק [אֶסְתֵּר ט, כב]
And so it is also mentioned in the pasuk (Esther 9:22):
"and the month which was turned for them
the whole month was turned to joy,
and this is not mentioned of the month of Nissan,
when in truth the redemption of Nissan is greater,
we are still servants of Achashveirosh."
The matter is that the redemption of Nissan
came from the side of Hashem Yisbarach,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [שְׁמוֹת ו, ו-ז] וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם וְגוֹמֵר
as it is said (Shemos 6:6–7), "And I will take you out," etc.,
"and I will take you to Me as a nation,
and I will be your God."
And so all the miracles were
from the side of Hashem Yisbarach,
Who struck Pharaoh and all of Egypt
and they were a blow to Egypt
in the manner expounded in the holy Zohar
that with each plague Hashem Yisbarach took
Yisrael out of one attribute of kelipah
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [דְּבָרִים ד, לד] גּוֹי מִקֶּרֶב גּוֹי
and as it is said (Devarim 4:34), "a nation from the midst of a nation,"
"the attribute of justice would not have allowed
Only Hashem Yisbarach took them out from among them,
like a fetus in its mother's womb.
וְכֵן בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף כְּתִיב [שְׁמוֹת יד, יד]
And so at the splitting of the Yam Suf it is written (Shemos 14:14):
all of it from the side of Hashem Yisbarach.
Which is not so with the month of Adar,
which was formed with the letter Kuf,
as is said in Sefer Yetzirah;
וְאוֹת ק׳ אִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (שַׁבָּת קד, א)
and of the letter Kuf it is brought in the Gemara (Shabbos 104a):
alluding to holiness from the side of Yisrael.
And so the eradication of Amalek was then carried out
and so the miracle was done
and the Jews killed in Shushan
הַצּוֹרְרִים וַעֲשֶׂרֶת בְּנֵי הָמָן [רְאֵה אֶסְתֵּר ט, ו-י]
the enemies and the ten sons of Haman (see Esther 9:6–10),
and in the other provinces of the king
the acceptance of the Torah she'b'al peh,
"They accepted it anew in the days of Achashveirosh" —
שֶׁעַל זֶה הָיָה כְּפִיַּית הָהָר כְּגִיגִית
that it was for this that the mountain was held over them like a barrel:
since it involves not so much hardship;
only regarding the Torah she'b'al peh,
עַל זֶה הָיָה כְּפִיַּית הַר כְּגִיגִית
for that the mountain was held over them like a barrel.
And in the days of Achashveirosh, out of love for the miracle,
they accepted it with joy, out of love (Rashi, Shabbos ibid.),
And from this comes the joy,
as they said in the Gemara (ibid.):
קָשְׁרוּ לְכָל אֶחָד שְׁנֵי כְתָרִים וְכוּלֵּי
they tied two crowns onto each one," etc.,
"and in the future Hakadosh Baruch Hu
will return them to us," etc.:
the joy of old upon their heads."
the yoke of His kingship, may He be blessed, on their own part,
And so it is written in the Megillah,
וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר [מִשְׁלֵי ו, כג] וְתוֹרָה אוֹר
and so it says (Mishlei 6:23), 'and Torah is light'" —
For the Torah she'b'chsav is called "or,"
which receives from the Torah she'b'chsav,
is in the aspect of the moon
And afterward it is written "and joy,"
which is like the crown of the joy of old.
is a crown upon the head,
"and every precious thing his eye beheld,"
וְאָמְרוּ (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה יט, ו, תַּנְחוּמָא חֻקַּת ח)
and they said (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:6, Tanchuma Chukas 8):
"This is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues:
רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וַחֲבֵירָיו
the eye of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues beheld
מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה
what the eye of Moshe did not behold."
And this is "the joy of old upon their heads,"
and this is what they said:
"When Adar enters we increase in joy."
And this is what they said afterward:
let him make himself available in Adar,
for after the eradication of Amalek
that it is bound to the root,
as they said in the holy Zohar
"in these three that depend on mazal,"
And this is why the Gemara says afterward
לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה [יִרְמְיָה כט, יא]
"'To give you a future and hope' (Yirmeyah 29:11) —
these are date palms and linen garments";
כְּרֵיחַ שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרְכוֹ ה׳ [בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז]
"'like the fragrance of a field which Hashem has blessed' (Bereishis 27:27) —
like the fragrance of a field of apples."
that since Rav Yehudah was quoted above,
לָמָּה נִסְמְכוּ שְׁתֵּי מֵימְרוֹת אֵלּוּ דַּיְיקָא
why specifically these two statements were placed together,
since there are other statements of his
And according to what was said,
דְּחֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ מְחִיַּית עֲמָלֵק
for the month of Adar, in which the eradication of Amalek took place —
that they are not all tzaddikim,
that among them too, even though they are circumcised,
which indicates the holiness of Yisrael,
that in truth "our will is to do Your will,
and who holds us back," etc.
And this is "its mazal is healthy,"
meaning they are bound at the root
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (מְגִילָּה ג, א)
along the lines of what they said (Megillah 3a):
אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִינְהוּ לָא חֲזוּ
for mazal is that which is
And on this it brought the exposition
"like the fragrance of a field," etc.,
דִּכְתִיב [בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, כז] וַיָּרַח אֶת רֵיחַ בְּגָדָיו
for it is written (Bereishis 27:27), "And he smelled the fragrance of his garments,"
and as they said in Bereishis Rabbah (ibid. 22):
that in truth they are all tzaddikim,
are only the clothing and garments of Esav,
they give off a good fragrance,
like the fragrance of a field of apples.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ סוֹד מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר [שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ז, ט]
this is the secret of what is said (Shir HaShirim 7:9):
"and the fragrance of your nose like apples":
for the fragrance of the nose alludes to the traitors,
דְּחָשַׁב (בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק לא, ג)
these are the waters of a person's nose" —
and nevertheless it gives off a good fragrance,
like apples, like a field of apples.
And so they brought the statement he said,
"'To give you a future and hope' —
these are date palms and linen garments,"
along the lines of what they said (Pesachim 87b):
for the main founding of the Torah she'b'al peh
see our words there at length);
And this is what is said (Yirmeyah 29:11):
that I think concerning you," etc.,
that in Adar its mazal is healthy,
for the engagement in holiness is from the side of Yisrael, as stated;
and on this it brought the statement
about date palms and linen garments,
which alludes to the Torah she'b'al peh
כָּל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לוֹ קְדוּשָּׁה
every one of Yisrael has holiness
and therefore the eradication of Amalek is in it.
And as our holy Rebbe said —
may the memory of the holy tzaddik be for a blessing
for the life of the World to Come —
that the villages read early, on the day of assembly:
since they engage in working the land;
and although the main eradication of Amalek
מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ בְּנֵי הַכְּפָרִים
nevertheless the amei ha'aretz too, the villagers,
that they are like the fragrance of a field of apples.
And on the contrary, they come first,
against Amalek's accusation is through them,
since he has claims against them,
to be bound at the root to Hashem Yisbarach,
that "our will is to do Your will,
and who holds us back," etc.
יֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
has a portion in the Torah she'b'al peh,
"and grant our portion in Your Torah,"
and as we have said many times
based on what they said (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3):
"'The congregation of Yannai' is not written here,
this refers to the amei ha'aretz.
And this was the portion of
(תַּנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רֵישׁ סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה, א)
(Tanna d'Vei Eliyahu, beginning of Seder Eliyahu Rabbah 1)
that Shabbos should be made entirely Torah.
And these three statements were said
in the name of Rav Yehudah son of
some studied Torah in Bnei Brak," etc. —
which concern the eradication of Amalek,
concerning the holiness of the bris;
and in Adar comes the clarification
and all are tzaddikim, as mentioned above;
and through being exiled to Bavel
they merited a good future and hope,
which is the root of the Torah she'b'al peh;
and they all give off a good fragrance,
like the fragrance of a field of apples,
for they are only the garments of Esav.
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (שָׁם לט, ב)
And along the lines of what they said in the Gemara (there, 39b):
and this is what people say:
comes the axe that goes into it'" —
so too Rav Yehudah son of
who was of the seed of Haman and Amalek,
which concern the eradication of Amalek in Adar,
on account of which we increase in joy in it.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 29a — “Rav Yehudah, son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, said in Rav's name: Just as, when Av enters, we reduce joy, so, when Adar enters, we increase joy.” The comparison of the two months is the premise of this maamar: Rav Tzadok asks why a month's distinctive event gives its character to the entire month.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Taanis 29a, s.v. MiShenichnas Adar — “When Adar enters—these were days of miracles for Israel: Purim and Pesach.” Rashi names both festivals. Rav Tzadok therefore examines whether the increase extends to Nisan, then distinguishes the particular quality of Adar.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 29b — “Rav Pappa said: Therefore, a Jewish person who has a lawsuit with a gentile should avoid him in Av, when his mazal is unfavorable, and make himself available in Adar, when his mazal is favorable.” The Gemara specifies Adar itself; this gives Rav Tzadok the textual basis for looking for a quality particular to Adar.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 29b–30a — “The one who says that the entire month is forbidden derives it from 'her month'; and the one who says that the entire week is forbidden derives it from 'her week.'” The preceding discussion records Rabbi Meir's restriction from Rosh Chodesh until the fast, Rabbi Yehudah's restriction throughout the month, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's restriction during the week. Rabbi Yochanan says that all three expound Hosea 2:13, 'I shall put an end to all her rejoicing, her festival, her month, and her week.' Rav Tzadok takes the month-long view as his comparison here.

paragraphs.text: Esther 9:22 — “As the days on which the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month that was transformed for them from sorrow to joy and from mourning to a festive day—to make them days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.” The verse speaks of the transformation of the month as well as the particular days. That wording supports the maamar's emphasis on Adar's whole-month character.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 14a — “Rav Nachman said: Reading the Megillah is its Hallel. Rava said: There, 'Praise, servants of Hashem' means that they are no longer Pharaoh's servants. But here, could we say 'Praise, servants of Hashem,' and not Ahasuerus's servants? We are still Ahasuerus's servants.” These are distinct explanations for the absence of a separate Hallel on Purim. Rav Tzadok invokes Rava's explanation to establish that the Exodus was the fuller political liberation, making Adar's special joy require a different explanation.

paragraphs.text: Exodus 6:6–7 — “Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am Hashem. I shall bring you out from under Egypt's burdens, rescue you from their service, and redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. I shall take you to Me as a people, and I shall be your God; you will know that I am Hashem your God, Who brings you out from under Egypt's burdens.” The repeated 'I shall' makes Divine initiative explicit. Rav Tzadok contrasts that initiative with the active acceptance and struggle undertaken by Israel in Adar.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 36a, Bo — “Rabbi Yosi said: In the very act in which judgment was found for the Egyptians, mercy was found for Israel, as it is written: 'I shall see the blood and pass over you.' So too, among all those holy crowns above, wherever judgment was found, mercy was found, all at the same moment. Rabbi Chizkiyah taught: 'Hashem shall strike Egypt, striking and healing'—striking Egypt and healing Israel. What is 'healing'? Since they had been circumcised, they needed healing.” The Zohar places judgment and mercy within the same act. The further correspondence of the successive plagues with successive measures of impurity and holiness is Rav Tzadok's development of this principle.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 23:2 — “Rabbi Elazar interpreted the verse concerning the redemption from Egypt: Just as a rose lying among thorns is difficult for its owner to pick, so it was difficult, as it were, for the Holy One, blessed be He, to redeem Israel. This is 'to take for Himself a nation from within a nation.' These were uncircumcised, and those were uncircumcised; these grew a forelock, and those grew a forelock; these wore forbidden mixtures, and those wore forbidden mixtures. Thus the attribute of judgment would never have allowed Israel to be redeemed from Egypt. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Had the Holy One, blessed be He, not bound Himself by an oath, Israel would never have been redeemed.” The Midrash explains the redemption as Divine intervention despite the apparent claims of strict judgment. It does not erase the distinction of Israel's identity; it describes the difficulty of their condition in Egypt.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 12 — “At the plague of the firstborn … Yisrael were shown to be bound at the root … but only for the moment; afterward, at the splitting of the Yam Suf, the prince of Egypt accused.” The parallel explains why the Nissan redemption had to come from Hashem alone. Yisrael's bond at the root was shown only for a moment, and the accusation that they were idolaters like Egypt was still open at the sea.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Yetzirah, Gra recension 5:10 — “He made the letter kuf rule over laughter, bound a crown to it, and combined them with one another. Through them He formed Pisces in the world, Adar in the year, and the spleen in the person, male and female.” This is the Gra recension, whose association of kuf, laughter, Adar, and the spleen matches the text used throughout these maamarim. The ordinary Warsaw recension has a different assignment of bodily organs.

paragraphs.text: Esther 9:6–10, 16 — “In Shushan the capital the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men, together with Parshandasa, Dalphon, Aspasa, Porasa, Adalya, Aridasa, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vayezasa, the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedasa, the enemy of the Jews. They did not lay their hands on the plunder.” Esther 9:16 further reports that the other Jews in the royal provinces defended their lives, rested from their enemies, and killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, without taking plunder. The verses identify Haman's sons and the attackers as Israel's enemies; the statement that all these enemies were Amalekites is Rav Tzadok's identification, rather than an explicit genealogical statement in these verses.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 88a — “'They stood at the foot of the mountain'—Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa said: This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, held the mountain over them like a tub and said: If you accept the Torah, well and good; if not, there shall be your grave. Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: From here there is a substantial plea concerning the Torah. Rava said: Nevertheless, they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus, as it is written: 'The Jews fulfilled and accepted'—they fulfilled what they had already accepted.” The renewed acceptance is stated in the Gemara. Its particular application to the Oral Torah is developed through the Midrash cited next.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3 — “If you say that He held the mountain over them on account of the Written Torah—had they not, as soon as He asked whether they accepted the Torah, all answered, 'We shall do and we shall hear'? For it does not involve such toil and hardship, and its extent is small. Rather, He spoke to them about the Oral Torah, which contains the fine distinctions of lighter and weightier commandments. It is strong as death, its ardor hard as the grave, for only one who loves the Holy One, blessed be He, with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might learns it. ‘You shall love Hashem your God with all your heart and all your soul and all your means’; afterward it says, ‘These words shall be upon your heart.’ Which is this? This is Talmud, which is upon the heart.” The contrast concerns the demanding labor of the Oral Torah. Rav Tzadok reads the Purim acceptance as a willing embrace of that labor.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 79b, Acharei Mos — “Concerning Channah it is written: 'She prayed above Hashem'—'above' precisely, because children depend on the holy mazal, as we have explained. There is no word in the Torah, or even a small letter in the Torah, that is not alluded to in supernal wisdom; from it hang countless mysteries of supernal wisdom.” The immediately following discussion reads 'Cast your burden above Hashem' precisely because sustenance depends on mazal, and it connects the added fifteen years of life with the same 'above.' Thus the three needs—children, sustenance, and life—are treated together. Rav Tzadok uses mazal for this supernal root, rather than simply for ordinary astrological prediction.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 17a — “Master of the universe, it is revealed and known before You that our desire is to do Your will. What prevents us? The leaven in the dough and the subjugation of kingdoms. May it be Your will to save us from their hands, so that we may return to perform the statutes of Your will with a whole heart.” Rabbi Alexandri's prayer distinguishes Israel's underlying desire from the internal and external obstacles to its expression. Rav Tzadok uses that distinction in answering Amalek's accusation.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 65:15 — “Esav the wicked becomes soiled by sins throughout the year and has no means of atonement; but Yaakov becomes soiled by sins throughout the year, Yom Kippur comes, and he has a means of atonement, as it is said: 'For on this day he shall atone.' Rabbi Yitzchak said: 'The goat shall bear upon itself'—this is Esav, as it is said, 'Esav my brother is a hairy man.' 'All their iniquities'—the iniquities of the wholehearted one, as it is said, 'Yaakov was a wholehearted man.'” The interpretation plays on se'ir, a goat or hairy one, and avonos tam, the sins of the wholehearted Yaakov. Rav Tzadok brings that transfer of accusation into his account of Israel's lasting root in holiness.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 65:22 — “Another interpretation of 'He smelled the fragrance of his garments and blessed him': such as Yosef Meshisa and Yakum of Tzeroros. When the enemies sought to enter the Temple Mount, they said: Let one of their own enter first. They told Yosef: Enter, and whatever you bring out is yours. He entered and brought out a golden Menorah. They told him: It is not fitting for an ordinary person to use this; enter a second time, and whatever you bring out is yours. He refused. They offered him three years of tax revenue, and he refused. He said: Is it not enough that I angered my God once, that I should anger Him a second time? They put him in a carpenter's frame and sawed him; he cried out: Woe, woe, that I angered my Creator.” The retrieved Midrash names him Yosef Meshisa; the manuscript's Yosi Meshisa is a name variant. His refusal to repeat his betrayal, despite coercion and inducement, supplies the concrete example of a concealed holy root becoming manifest.

paragraphs.text: Avos DeRabbi Nasan 31:3 — “He fashioned in the human being everything that He created in His world. ... He created fragrance in the world and fragrance in the human being—this is the person's nose. ... Foul water in the world, foul water in the human being—this is the fluid of the person's nose. Salt water in the world, salt water in the human being—these are the tears of the eyes.” The source is a catalogue of correspondences between the world and the body. Rav Tzadok selects the nose's seemingly disagreeable fluid while interpreting 'the fragrance of your nose like apples,' showing how a hidden root can yield fragrance.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 87b–88a — “Ulla said: So that they should eat dates and occupy themselves with Torah. Ulla came to Pumbedisa, and they brought him a basket of dates. He asked: How many like this can be bought for a zuz? They said: Three for a zuz. He said: A basketful of honey for a zuz, and the Babylonians do not occupy themselves with Torah!” The opening words of Ulla's answer, 'So that they should eat,' are at the end of 87b; 'dates and occupy themselves with Torah' continues on 88a. The statement explains exile to Bavel in terms of the material conditions that enable Torah study.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Mishpatim 1 — “In the Babylonian exile the principal establishment of the Oral Torah took place through the Men of the Great Assembly, and likewise in the generations afterward. ... Subsequently, in the days of the Amoraim, came the Babylonian Talmud, which is the principal Oral Torah that we possess. ... This is the good future. As for 'palm trees and linen garments,' it may mean what they said: they were exiled to Bavel so that they might eat dates and engage in Torah. ... Linen garments correspond to 'He showed me the Torah scholars of Bavel resembling ministering angels'; Rashi explains that they wore white. ... Since the place does not have the holiness of the Land, they require the holiness of garments.” This is the author's own cross-reference, retrieved from the Lublin 1901 text. It explains exactly why the two concrete gifts—dates and linen—can signify the flourishing of the Oral Torah in exile.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 2a — “The Megillah is read on the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth—not earlier and not later. Cities surrounded by a wall since the days of Yehoshua bin Nun read on the fifteenth. Villages and large towns read on the fourteenth, except that the villages advance their reading to the day of gathering.” The Gemara explains that the Sages granted this leniency so villagers could supply water and food to their brothers in the cities. The villagers as an image of the unlearned, and their priority in answering Amalek's accusation, are the interpretation transmitted here by Rav Tzadok in the name of his teacher.

paragraphs.text: Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 1 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: Did I not write for you in My Torah, 'This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth'? Even though you work through all six days, Shabbos should be made entirely Torah. From here they said: A person should rise early on Shabbos, review his learning, and go to the synagogue and study hall; he should read Torah and study the Prophets. Afterward he should go home, eat, and drink, fulfilling 'Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a good heart.'” The instruction specifically addresses those occupied with labor during the week. The same passage includes eating and drinking, so 'entirely Torah' describes Shabbos's governing purpose rather than the exclusion of its meals.

paragraphs.text: Ein Yaakov, Sanhedrin 96b — “Descendants of Sisera learned Torah in Jerusalem. Descendants of Sancheriv taught Torah in public—and who were they? Shemayah and Avtalyon. Descendants of Haman learned Torah in Bnei Brak—and who was it? Rav Shmuel bar Shilas.” The final identification with Rav Shmuel bar Shilas is present in the retrieved Ein Yaakov text. The standard Sanhedrin text retrieved for comparison reports Haman's descendants learning in Bnei Brak without naming him. Rav Tzadok explicitly relies on the Ein Yaakov reading.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 39b — “Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let Ovadiah, who lived between two wicked people and did not learn from their deeds, come and prophesy against Esav the wicked, who lived between two righteous people and did not learn from their deeds. Ephraim Maksha'ah, Rabbi Meir's student, said in Rabbi Meir's name: Ovadiah was an Edomite convert. This is the popular saying: From the forest itself comes the wood for the axe that enters it.” The source explains why Ovadiah is appointed to prophesy against Edom. Rav Tzadok applies its pattern to a teaching transmitted through a descendant of Haman that overturns Amalek's accusation.
